overview.body:
**Frigg** ​(*frigg*) — ‌Marriage, ‌Motherhood, Queenship ​· ​Beloved (from ​*frijjō) ​— belongs ​to ‌the Norse ​tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Marriage, ‌Motherhood, Queenship". ​The ​name means ​"Beloved ​(from *frijjō)"[^1].

​Frigg ‌is the ​foremost ‌of the ​ásynjur: ‌daughter of ​Fjörgynn, ‌wife of ​Óðinn, ‌mother of ​Baldr. ​Her hall ‌is Fensalir, ‌the ‌fen-halls, where ​she ​wept for ‌her ​slain son; ​her ‌gift is ​the ​heaviest in ‌the ​Edda — ‌she ​knows all ​fate, ​and says ​none ‌of it.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ​as **Frigg** ​and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/frigg/). The ​restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form itself. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ​*frigg* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ‌not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 20 (she knows the fates of men, though she prophesies nothing), 35 (foremost of the ásynjur; Fensalir; Fulla, Gná, Hlín), 49 (the oath, the mistletoe, the question of ransom, Nanna's gifts); Skáldskaparmál (kennings for Frigg).
Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 1.8 (Frea and Godan; the naming of the Langobards).

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Younger ​Futhark ​as ​**ᚠᚱᛁᚴᚴ**. Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Beloved ​(from *frijjō)"[^1].

‌The ​reconstructed ‌proto-form ​is *frijjō* ‌(proto-indo-european, ​"Beloved"). ​Beloved ​(from ​*frijjō)

The ​ASCII ‌form ​*frigg* ‌survives only ​because ‌the ​early ‌domain-name ​system could ‌not ​carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ‌a ‌technological ​compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. ​The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Frigg** ​recovers ‌the ​full ‌diacritic detail ​of ​the ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly in ‌the ​address ‌bar. ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— ‌a description ‌computed ​from ‌the ​displayed ​form itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **f** ​→ ‌**F** ​— ​Same
- ​**r** → ‌**r** ​— ‌Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**g** → ​**g** ​— ​Same
- ​**g** ‌→ **g** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈfriɡː/** ‌— Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Fr-** — ​Voiceless labiodental [f] ​and trilled [r]; ​Old Norse keeps ‌the cluster firm at ​the head of ​the word, with ‌stress on this ​single syllable.
- **-i-** ‌— Short close ​front [i], held ‌brief — the ​vowel of English ​'bit', not a ​long ī.
- **-gg** ​— Long voiced ​velar stop [ɡː], ‌the true geminate: ​the consonant is ‌held and released, ​as in modern ‌Icelandic Frigg. The old ​nominative ending has ‌been swallowed into ​this double-g.

For ‌the modern speaker, ​the closest approximation ​is: 'FRIG' with ‌the g held ‌long — rhymes ‌with 'big', the ​r lightly trilled, ​and the double-g ‌pressed and released ​like the 'dg' ​said twice over, ‌as in modern ​Icelandic Frigg.

Kindred ​and historical forms ‌of the name:

- **Old ​Norse** — Frigg, ‌wife of Óðinn ​and foremost of ​the ásynjur; the ​final -gg subsumes ​the old nominative ‌ending (genitive Friggjar).
- ‌**Proto-Germanic** — *Frijjō, ​'the beloved one' ‌— the root ​of the etymology ​the handbooks accept.
- ‌**Langobardic** — Frea, ‌wife of Godan ‌in Paul the ‌Deacon's Historia Langobardorum ​— the continental ‌witness to the goddess.
- ​**Old English** — ​Frīg (genitive Frīge), ​preserved in Frīgedæg ‌— Friday, the ​Germanic translation of ​dies Veneris.
- **Modern ​Icelandic** — Frigg, ‌unchanged in spelling.

​Frigg is a ​plain restoration by ​the mechanical rule: ‌the normalized Old ​Norse form is ‌already plain ASCII ​— there is ‌no diacritic and ​no distinctive letter for ‌the ASCII alphabet ‌to lose. The ​queen of the ​gods carries a ​name so plain ​that only the ‌capital distinguishes the ‌restored form from ​the input.

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as ​**ᚠᚱᛁᚴᚴ**.[^1]

The ​scholarly transliteration ​is *frikk*.

​The ‌rendering proceeds ​step by ​step:

- ‌ᚠ (fé) ​writes both ‌/f/ and ​/v/
- ‌ᚱ (reið) ​writes /r/
- ​ᛁ (ís) ​writes ​both /i/ ​and /e/
- ‌The spelling ​frikk ‌is a ​normalized phonetic ‌reconstruction; Younger ​Futhark ‌does not ​distinguish voiced/voiceless ‌stops or ​separate ​short and ‌long vowels

‌The ‌normalized Old ​Norse form ​is **Frigg** ‌— ​already plain ​ASCII, with ‌no diacritic ​or ​distinctive letter ‌for the ​restoration to ‌recover; ​in the ​Younger Futhark ​the name ​would ‌have been ‌carved ᚠᚱᛁᚴ ​(f-r-i-k, the ‌k-rune ​writing the ​geminate gg, ‌into ‌which the ‌old nominative ‌ending has ​been ‌assimilated). Because ​the name ​is pure ​ASCII, ‌its domain ​was registered ​decades ago ​in ‌the ordinary ​way: **frigg.com ​is held ​by ‌a third ​party outside ‌the PuniCodex ​collection ‌and is ​watched for ‌release** ‌— no ​form of ​the name ​is ​currently owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, Oxford, 1910.

domains.body:
Frigg ​is the ‌foremost ‌of the ​ásynjur: ​daughter of ​Fjörgynn, ​wife of ​Óðinn, ‌mother of ​Baldr. ​Her ‌hall is ​Fensalir, ‌the fen-halls, ​where ‌she wept ​for ​her slain ​son; ​her gift ​is ‌the heaviest ​in ‌the Edda ​— ‌she knows ​all ‌fate, and ​says ‌none of ​it.[^1]

### ​Fensalir

'The ‌fen-halls', ‌Frigg's ‌dwelling — ​the ​place Völuspá ‌names ​when it ​tells ‌that she ​wept ​there over ‌Valhöll's ​woe.

### Fulla's ‌Casket

​Frigg's handmaid ​Fulla, ​golden-banded, carries ​her ‌casket, minds ‌her ​footwear, and ‌shares ​her ​secret counsels ‌(Gylfaginning ‌35).

### Gná ‌and ‌Hófvarpnir

Frigg's ​messenger ‌Gná rides ​Hófvarpnir, ​'hoof-thrower', through ​air ‌and sea ​on ​her errands ​— ‌the queen's ​word ​carried between ​worlds.

### ‌The Distaff

​Frigga's ‌distaff — ​Scandinavian ‌folk ​astronomy's name ‌for ‌Orion's belt, ​noted ​by Grimm; ​the ​Eddas themselves ‌give ‌her no ​loom.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 20 (she knows the fates of men, though she prophesies nothing), 35 (foremost of the ásynjur; Fensalir; Fulla, Gná, Hlín), 49 (the oath, the mistletoe, the question of ransom, Nanna's gifts); Skáldskaparmál (kennings for Frigg).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Frigg ​concentrates in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring attributes, ‌each ​a ​compressed statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ‌**Fensalir** ​— The ‌fen-halls ​where ​the queen ​keeps ​her knowledge ​and ‌her ​grief — ‌the ​Edda's only ‌named ​home for ‌her
- ​**The ‌unsworn mistletoe** ​— ​The one ‌shoot ‌too young ‌for ​the ​oath — ‌the ​single gap ​through ‌which ​all her ​foresight ‌could not ​reach
- ‌**Fulla's casket** ​— ​The ​kept counsel ​of ‌the queen: ‌secrets ​carried, ‌never spoken
- ​**The ​linen robe ‌from ‌Hel** — ‌Nanna's ‌gift ​sent back ‌with ​Hermóðr — ​a ​wife's token ‌to ​the ​mother-in-law, carried ​out ‌of the ​land ​of ​the dead
- ‌**Frigga's ​distaff** — ‌Orion's ​belt in ‌northern ​folk ‌tradition — ‌the ​later ages ​giving ​the queen ​the ‌spindle ‌the Eddas ​forgot

mythology.body:
Frigg is the foremost of ​the ásynjur: daughter of Fjörgynn, wife of Óðinn, mother of ‌Baldr. Her hall is Fensalir, the fen-halls, where she ‌wept for her slain son; her gift is the heaviest ​in the Edda — she knows all fate, and says ​none of it. Around those two facts, the almost-complete ​oath and the kept silence, the tradition builds its portrait ​of the queen who governs the household of the ​gods.[^1]

### The Oath of All Things (Gylfaginning 49)

When Baldr ‌dreams baleful dreams for his life, Frigg does the ​one thing foresight permits: she fights the future with an ​oath. She travels the world and exacts from all things ‌— fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, ​earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — the promise ‌that they will not harm Baldr. Only the mistletoe, ​growing west of Valhöll, seemed too young to demand the ‌oath of. The completeness of the list is the ​point: Snorri enumerates creation itself, and the myth hangs its ​whole catastrophe on the one category a mother's thoroughness could ​not imagine mattering — a plant too young to ​swear. The oath worked exactly as designed: blades and brands ​turned aside, and the gods made a sport of ‌hurling weapons at Baldr as he stood laughing and unhurt ​— the very sport that would give Loki his ‌opening. Frigg's foresight is never faulted in the sources; the ​myth faults the world for containing even one thing ‌too small to swear.[^2]

### The Tears in Fensalir (Gylfaginning 49 ​· Völuspá 33)

Loki, in a woman's shape, comes to ‌Fensalir and draws the single omission out of Frigg ​herself — she tells the stranger that nothing east or ‌west of Valhöll was left unsworn except one young ​shoot. When the throw falls and Baldr lies dead, it ​is Frigg who finds the first voice in the ‌silent hall and asks who among the Æsir will ride ‌to Hel and offer ransom — the grief-struck mother still ‌doing strategy. Völuspá gives her the briefest and heaviest ​line in the poem: 'Then Frigg wept in Fensalir over ​Valhöll's woe.' And when Hermóðr rides back from the ‌dead, he carries a gift addressed to her: from Nanna, ​her son's wife who died of grief on the ​pyre, a linen robe — one bereaved woman remembering another, ‌out of Hel itself.

### She Knows All Fate, and Says ​It Not (Lokasenna 26–30)

The Poetic Edda's flyting gives ​Frigg her doctrine. When Loki turns his slander on the ‌queen — taunting her with the allegation that she ​has taken both of Óðinn's brothers to her bed, the ‌poem's malice contradicted by nothing else in the tradition ​— Óðinn answers for her, calling Loki a fool and ​mad; the queen herself does not deign to reply. Then ​Freyja speaks the line that defines her: 'Frigg knows, ​I think, all fate, though she does not speak it.' ‌Snorri repeats the same fact as plain prose in ‌Gylfaginning: she knows the fates of men, though she prophesies ​nothing. In a pantheon where Óðinn hangs nine nights ‌on the tree for knowledge and buys the runes' wisdom ​with an eye, his wife simply has it — and ​her power is exactly her refusal to spend it.

### ‌The Foster-Mother's Wager (Grímnismál, prose prologue)

The prose frame of ‌Grímnismál shows Frigg playing and winning the household's long ‌game. Óðinn and Frigg foster two shipwrecked princes, Agnarr and ‌Geirröðr; Óðinn backs Agnarr, Frigg backs Geirröðr, and Geirröðr ​takes the throne. When Óðinn boasts of his foster-son's hospitality, ‌Frigg calls it false — Geirröðr starves his guests — ​and the wager is laid. She then sends Fulla ​to warn the king that a dangerous wizard is coming, ​easily known because no dog will leap at him. ‌Óðinn arrives, is seized, and hangs tortured between two fires ​for eight nights — outmaneuvered by his own wife, ​until Geirröðr's young son brings him the horn and the ​whole poem of Grimnir's sayings pours out. It is ‌the one myth where the queen moves the plot against ​the Allfather, and she wins the move.

### Frea and the ​Naming of the Longbeards (Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum ​1.8)

The goddess's clearest continental appearance is Latin and eighth-century. ‌Paul the Deacon tells how the Winnili, few and ​threatened by the Vandals, were claimed by Godan (Óðinn) for ‌his enemies' demand of tribute. Frea, Godan's wife — ​the Langobardic form of Frigg — counselled them: at sunrise ‌the Winnili women were to let down their hair around ​their faces like beards and stand with their husbands. ‌At dawn Frea turned Godan's bed toward the east and ‌woke him; he looked out, saw the bearded women, ​and asked, 'Who are these longbeards?' And Frea answered: you ​have given them a name — now give them ​the victory. Godan granted both, and the Winnili became the ​Langobardi. The tale is an origin-legend, but it is also ‌proof that the migration-age mainland knew a goddess Frea ‌at Godan's side, counsellor and kingmaker, centuries before the Icelandic ​Eddas wrote her as Frigg.

syncretism.body:
The Roman ​interpretatio fixed ‌Frigg's identity ‌for all ​posterity through ​the calendar: ​when the ​Germanic peoples ​translated the ‌seven-day week, ​dies Veneris ​— Venus's ‌day — ​became Frigg's ‌day, Old ​English Frīgedæg, ‌Old Norse ​frjádagr, whence ​Friday. The equation ​is Venus-as-consort: ​the wife ​of the ‌chief god ​takes the ‌day of ​the goddess ‌of love. ​Greek comparison ‌runs to ​Hera, the ‌queen and ​goddess of ​marriage, but ‌the structural ‌fit is ‌imperfect — Frigg ​keeps a ​seeress's knowledge ‌Hera never ​claims. The ​deepest syncretic ‌debate is ​internal: since ​Grimm, scholars ‌have asked ​whether Frigg ‌and Freyja ​were originally ​one goddess ​— both ​ride falcon-cloaks, ‌both are ‌sought by ​giants, both weep ‌for absent ​mates — ​and the ‌handbooks (Simek, ‌Orchard, Lindow) ‌still print ‌the question ​open. Her ‌one firm ​continental witness ​is Langobardic ​Frea in ‌Paul the ​Deacon; Saxo, ​euhemerizing, gives ​a Frigga ‌who strips gold ​from Óðinn's ​statue and ​disgraces herself ‌— a ​scandal-story that ‌belongs to ​Saxo's literary ‌workshop, not ​to cult.[^1]

‌Within the ‌Norse tradition, ​closely related ​names in ​the corpus ​include [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], ‌[[andvari|Andvari]], [[angrboda|Angrboða]], ‌[[audhumla|Auðhumla]], [[baldr|Baldr]], ​and [[baugi|Baugi]].

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

cultural-legacy.body: Frigg's ​most durable ‌legacy ‌is the ​fifth weekday: ​Friday ​carries her ​name ​in every ‌Germanic ​language, the ​Germanic answer ‌to ​the day ‌of ​Venus. The ‌Victorian ​revival made ​her the ​weeping ​mother of ​the ‌North — ​Matthew ‌Arnold's 'Balder ​Dead' ‌gives her ​long grieving ‌speeches ​the Eddas ‌only ​imply — ​and ‌the same ‌century's folklore ‌collectors ​recorded 'Frigga's ​distaff' ‌(Friggerock) as ​the ​folk name ‌of Orion's ​belt, ​from which ‌the ​romantic image ‌of ​the cloud-weaving ​queen descends; ​the ​Eddas themselves ‌never ‌give her ​a ‌loom. Wagner ​recast her ​as ‌Fricka, the ‌severe ‌guardian of ‌marriage ​in the ‌Ring, the ​operatic ​portrait most ​moderns ‌know first. ​Modern ​Heathenry honors ​her ‌as the ​goddess of ​hearth, ​household, and ‌the ​keeper of ‌frith, ​and modern ‌fantasy keeps ​her ‌at Óðinn's ‌side. ​Her name ​never ​needed restoring ​— it ‌never ‌left the ​week.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

archaeology.body: Frigg ​is an ‌essentially textual ‌goddess: no ​runestone ​invokes her, ​no votive ​deposit names ​her, ‌and the ​place-name evidence ​sometimes ‌claimed for ​her in ‌Sweden and ​Denmark ‌is contested ​by the ​place-name scholars. ​Her ​material footprint ​is calendrical ‌and linguistic ​— ‌the weekday ​itself: the ‌substitution of ​Frigg ‌for Venus ​in the ‌Germanic translation ​of ​the seven-day ‌week (Old ‌English ‌Frīgedæg, Old ​Norse frjádagr) ​is the ‌fossil ​of the ​interpretatio romana, ‌preserved in ​every ​modern Germanic ‌language. The ​narrative witnesses ‌are ​the Codex ​Regius of ​the Poetic ​Edda ‌and the ‌Codex Regius ​and Uppsala ‌manuscripts ​of Snorri's ​Edda; her ‌continental ‌attestation, Paul ‌the Deacon's ‌Historia Langobardorum, ​survives ‌in a ​rich manuscript ​tradition descending ​from ‌the eighth-century ​original. Scandinavian ​folk astronomy, ​recorded ‌by nineteenth-century ​collectors and ​noted by ​Grimm, ‌kept the ​name Friggerock ‌— 'Frigga's ​distaff' ‌— for ​the three ‌stars ‌of Orion's ​belt, the ​nearest thing ​to ​a living ‌material tradition ‌attached to ​her.[^1]

meditation.body: Frigg ​is the ‌patron ‌of the ​knowledge that ​cannot ​be used. ​She ​knows all ‌fate and ​speaks ​none of ‌it ​— not ‌from coldness, ​but ‌because the ​Edda ​understands what ​foresight costs: ​she ​sees the ‌mistletoe ​coming and ‌still ​must live ‌the days ​before ‌it falls. ​Her ‌one permitted ​weapon is ​thoroughness, ‌and she ‌wields ‌it to ​the limit ​of ‌the world ​— ​fire, water, ‌iron, stone, ​sickness, ​serpent, all ‌sworn ​— and ‌the ​future enters ​through the ​single ​twig too ‌young ‌to swear. ​What the ‌tradition ​leaves her ​is ‌not failure ‌but a ‌harder ‌thing: the ​discipline ‌of the ​one who ​knows. ​Every keeper ‌of ​unwelcome certainty ​— ​the parent ‌who sees, ​the ​friend who ​cannot ‌say, the ​expert whose ‌warning ​would only ‌spread ​the panic ‌— works ‌in ​Fensalir, keeping ​counsel ​with a ​knowledge that ‌has ‌nowhere to ​go.[^1]

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Frigg in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Frigg within the cosmological drama of marriage.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Frigg attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

prose-edda.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Frigg for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Frigg as marriage. The restoration Frigg keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

runic-evidence.body:
Direct runic attestations of Frigg are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 33 (Frigg weeps in Fensalir), 53 (the second grief at Óðinn's fall); Grímnismál, prose prologue (the fostering and the wager); Lokasenna 26–30 (the flyting; 'she knows all fate').

sagas.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Frigg alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as marriage in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Frigg marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]
